articles.title: Impact of donor size on short- and long-term outcomes in pediatric kidney transplant recipients: where is the mismatch limit? Analysis of the Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients database.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND HYPOTHESIS: The impact of kidney size mismatch on outcomes after pediatric kidney transplantation remains poorly understood. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of donor-recipient height mismatch on short- and long-term outcomes in pediatric kidney transplant recipients. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients (SRTR), including pediatric kidney transplant recipients between 2010 and 2020. The primary endpoint was graft loss; secondary endpoints were overall survival, acute rejection, and kidney function. Hazard ratios were calculated using Fine and Gray's proportional subdistribution hazards models. RESULTS: A total of 5321 patients were included (mean age 10.4 ± 5.2 years). A higher donor to recipient height ratio was associated with an increased risk of graft loss (HR 1.90; 95% CI 1.09-3.30; p = 0.023). However, this adverse effect decreased with increasing recipient age (interaction age × HD/Rr: HR 0.93; 95% CI 0.88-0.99; p = 0.016). No significant differences were observed regarding acute rejection or overall survival. CONCLUSION: Donor-recipient height mismatch increases the risk of graft loss in children; but this adverse effect diminished with recipient age. While height matching should be prioritized in early childhood, flexible allocation, including the use of larger adult living donor organs, remains a sound clinical strategy in children with chronic kidney disease stage 5, as the benefits of transplantation outweigh the risk of size mismatch.

articles.title: Risk factors for congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT) are a leading cause of pediatric renal failure. This study evaluated risk factors and assessed their robustness. METHODS: PubMed, EMBASE, and Scopus searches yielded 33 studies (24 case-control, 9 cohort). Frequentist and Bayesian random-effects meta-analyses estimated associations between CAKUT and maternal/neonatal risks. RESULTS: Frequentist analysis identified increased risk for pre-pregnancy BMI 25.0-29.9 (OR, 1.24; 95% CI, 1.06-1.45), ≥30 (OR, 1.27; 95% CI, 1.07-1.51), and ≥25 kg/m² (OR, 1.24; 95% CI, 1.11-1.37). Maternal age <20 years was protective (OR, 0.61; 95% CI, 0.51-0.73). Other predictors included family history of CAKUT/kidney disease, maternal diabetes subtypes (type 1, type 2, pre-gestational, and gestational diabetes), preterm birth (OR, 1.59; 95% CI, 1.25-2.03), small-for-gestational-age (SGA), and large-for-gestational-age (LGA). Bayesian analysis validated most factors. Although 95% CrIs crossed unity for BMI 25.0-29.9 kg/m², BMI ≥ 30 kg/m², T2DM, SGA, LGA, alcohol consumption, RASi use, and hypertension, their posterior distributions were predominantly above 1. High BMI, family history, and diabetes remained robust in high-quality subsets. CONCLUSIONS: Confirming established risks and identifying novel associations, these findings identify maternal metabolic factors as consistent correlates of CAKUT and support their evaluation as potentially modifiable targets. IMPACT: Current meta-analyses lack synthesis on novel CAKUT determinants (maternal exposures, comorbidities, gestational weight gain, extreme fetal weight) and Bayesian approaches, which are essential to robustly address heterogeneity in sparse data. Our frequentist analysis confirmed established risks and identified novel associations: family history, SGA, LGA, and type 1 and 2 diabetes. Bayesian meta-analysis supported the main findings and showed posterior probabilities that OR > 1 of ≥90% for BMI subgroups, T2DM, RASi use, and hypertension. Maternal metabolic factors are consistently associated with CAKUT and represent potentially modifiable targets that warrant evaluation in future prospective and interventional studies.

articles.title: Low serum testosterone concentrations predict incident frailty in men with HIV.
articles.abstract: CONTEXT: Older men with HIV (MWH) experience a higher burden of frailty than age-matched men without HIV, but the biological mechanisms underlying this vulnerability are not completely understood. Testosterone (T) deficiency may contribute to frailty through effects on muscle mass and physical function. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the associations of free T, total T, and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) with incident frailty among MWH. METHODS: Three hundred six nonfrail MWH (129 robust and 177 prefrail) with longitudinal frailty assessments from the Multicenter AIDS Cohort Study and Women's Interagency HIV Study Combined Cohort Study were enrolled. Incident frailty defined using the Fried frailty phenotype. Free T, total T, and SHBG were measured, with free T assessed by equilibrium dialysis. Marginal structural models were used to estimate associations with frailty outcomes while accounting for time and related covariates. RESULTS: Over a mean follow-up of 9.0 years, low free T (<54 pg/mL) and low total T (<300 ng/dL) were associated with higher risk of incident frailty compared with higher concentrations (hazard ratio [HR]: 2.49, 95% CI: 1.21-5.11; HR: 3.31, 95% CI: 1.26-8.68, respectively). Sex hormone-binding globulin concentrations were not consistently associated with frailty outcomes. CONCLUSION: Low T levels predict incident frailty in MWH. Assessment of androgen status may help identify men at increased frailty risk. Further investigations are warranted to assess the role of T therapy in frailty prevention.
articles.journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism

articles.title: Incident hyperkalaemia risk model in chronic kidney disease and diabetes: the FIDELITY programme.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: No tools are available for identifying patients with chronic kidney disease and Type 2 diabetes at high risk of hyperkalaemia. Using the FIDELITY pooled patient data set, a risk model for incident hyperkalaemia was developed and validated. METHODS: The primary outcome was new-onset hyperkalaemia (serum potassium >5.5 mmol/L). Data from the placebo arm were used for derivation and from the finerenone arm for validation. An integer risk score was built and divided into low-, intermediate-, and high-risk hyperkalaemia categories. Assessed efficacy outcomes included cardiovascular and kidney composites. RESULTS: Seven baseline covariates (serum potassium >4.5 mmol/L, prior history of hyperkalaemia, no sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 inhibitor use, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio >1000 mg/g, haemoglobin <12 g/dL, no thiazide-type diuretic use, and estimated glomerular filtration rate <45 mL/min/1.73 m2) were independently associated with new-onset hyperkalaemia and used for building the integer risk model. The risk scores for derivation and validation were accurate and well calibrated. The derived integer score ranged from 0 to 12 points. The risk of new-onset hyperkalaemia increased across hyperkalaemia risk categories with 2.7, 7.0, and 16.7% of patients reporting a hyperkalaemia event in the low-risk (0-3 points), intermediate-risk (4-6 points), and high-risk (7-12 points) groups with placebo, respectively. Irrespective of hyperkalaemia risk, finerenone reduced cardiovascular and kidney events vs placebo. CONCLUSIONS: This integer risk score for new-onset hyperkalaemia in patients with chronic kidney disease and Type 2 diabetes could facilitate tailored treatment strategies and mitigate hyperkalaemia in high-risk patients.

articles.title: Renal Insufficiency and Clinical Outcomes in Acute Ischemic Stroke With Large Infarct: A Prospective Cohort Analysis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: This study aimed to investigate whether renal insufficiency (RI) modifies the effectiveness and safety of endovascular treatment (EVT) in patients with acute ischemic stroke and large infarct in a real-world setting. METHODS: This study was a post hoc analysis of a prospective multicenter cohort study. RI was defined as an estimated glomerular filtration rate <90 mL/min per 1.73 m2 on admission. Patients were treated with EVT plus standard medical treatment or standard medical treatment alone and were stratified by RI status. The primary effectiveness outcome was favorable outcome (modified Rankin scale 0-3) at 90 days. Safety outcomes included symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage and 90-day mortality. RESULTS: Among 745 patients with acute ischemic stroke and large infarct, 343 (46.0%) had RI and 490 (65.8%) underwent EVT. Compared with standard medical treatment, EVT was associated with improved functional outcomes (modified Rankin scale 0-3) in both the RI (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 2.55 [95% CI, 1.15-5.68], P=0.022) and the non-RI group (adjusted OR 2.65 [95% CI, 1.49-4.73], P=0.001). EVT was also associated with higher risks of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage in both groups (P=0.002 and 0.007, respectively), whereas no significant difference in mortality was observed. Results were consistent in the inverse probability-weighted analyses. No statistically significant interaction was observed between RI status and treatment effect for effectiveness or safety outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: In patients with acute ischemic stroke and large infarct, EVT was associated with improved functional outcomes but a higher risk of hemorrhagic complications. We did not find statistically significant evidence of interaction between EVT and RI status for 90-day outcomes.
articles.journal: Journal of the American Heart Association

articles.title: Associations between urate‑lowering strategies and kidney function trajectories: a real‑world comparative study.
articles.abstract: Hyperuricemia contributes to chronic kidney disease progression, yet whether different urate-lowering agents are associated with distinct kidney function trajectories remains unclear. This retrospective cohort study evaluated the associations between dotinurad, a selective urate transporter 1 (URAT1) inhibitor, and kidney function trajectories compared with benzbromarone and allopurinol. Adults treated with uric acid lowering agents (ULAs) at a university hospital between January 2021 and April 2024 were included. The primary outcome was annual change in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). Secondary outcomes included rapid eGFR decline (≥4 mL/min/1.73 m2/year) and sustained eGFR decline (≥10% from baseline). Among 605 patients (median follow-up 369 days), adjusted mixed-effects analyses estimated annual eGFR slopes of -1.58, -1.87, and -0.78 mL/min/1.73 m2/year for allopurinol, benzbromarone, and dotinurad, respectively, with no significant between-group differences. Rapid eGFR decline occurred in 16.8%, 26.2%, and 12.2% of patients receiving allopurinol, benzbromarone, and dotinurad, respectively. In multivariable logistic regression, compared with benzbromarone, both dotinurad (odds ratio [OR]: 0.34, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.16-0.75) and allopurinol (OR: 0.55, 95% CI: 0.31-0.99) were associated with lower odds of rapid eGFR decline. Sensitivity analyses using alternative decline thresholds (≥3 or ≥5 mL/min/1.73 m2/year) yielded similar findings. In Cox analyses, compared with benzbromarone, dotinurad was associated with a lower hazard of sustained eGFR decline (hazard ratio [HR]: 0.46, 95% CI: 0.24-0.88). These findings suggest potential differences in kidney outcomes across urate-lowering strategies.

articles.title: Deconstructing ERAS: A nomogram for predicting short- to intermediate-term stone recurrence after PCNL.
articles.abstract: Although percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) is highly effective for managing complex renal calculi, postoperative recurrence remains a substantial clinical challenge. Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocols consistently improve short-term perioperative outcomes; however, their potential relationship with subsequent stone recurrence remains poorly understood. This retrospective cohort study, conducted between January and June 2023, evaluated 200 patients undergoing PCNL. We aimed to determine whether specific ERAS components were associated with short- to intermediate-term recurrence and to develop an exploratory nomogram for postoperative risk stratification. The standard ERAS pathway was deconstructed into 10 dichotomous variables. The primary composite outcome was new stone formation or clinically significant residual fragment growth occurring 6 to 24 months postoperatively. The overall recurrence rate was 31.0%. Following backward stepwise multivariable logistic regression, five independent predictors were retained in the final model: metabolic syndrome (OR 4.053), stone surface area (OR 1.004), preoperative counseling (OR 0.163), opioid-free anesthesia (OR 0.256), and early tube removal (OR 0.050, functioning as a prognostic proxy for an uncomplicated surgical course). The resulting nomogram demonstrated promising internal discrimination, yielding an area under the curve of 0.939, alongside acceptable internal calibration via bootstrap resampling. Decision curve analysis suggested potential net clinical utility. In conclusion, the prognostic relevance of ERAS in PCNL relies upon specific clinical components rather than the generalized protocol. This preliminary nomogram provides an individualized tool to assist in postoperative risk stratification and hypothesis generation for future prospective validation.

articles.title: Effect modification of the association between vancomycin trough concentration and acute kidney injury: A retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: Vancomycin exposure is associated with acute kidney injury (AKI), but the extent to which concomitant clinical factors modify this association remains uncertain. This study evaluated factors associated with vancomycin-related AKI and examined potential effect modification of the association between vancomycin trough concentration and AKI. This single-center retrospective cohort study used electronic health records of adults treated with vancomycin from January 2019 to June 2023. Factors associated with AKI were assessed using logistic regression, and interaction terms were used to evaluate whether the trough-AKI association differed according to selected comorbidities and concomitant medications. A systematic review and meta-analysis were also performed to place the cohort findings in the context of existing evidence. Among 1612 patients, 375 (23.2%) developed AKI. Higher vancomycin trough concentration, concomitant loop diuretic use, and concomitant piperacillin/tazobactam (PIP/TAZ) use were independently associated with AKI. Statistically significant interactions with trough concentration were observed for PIP/TAZ, chronic kidney disease, hypertension, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor/angiotensin-receptor blocker use (interaction P = .036, .023, .003, and .006, respectively). Compared with patients not receiving PIP/TAZ and with trough levels < 17 mg/L, the odds of AKI were higher among patients receiving PIP/TAZ with trough levels < 17 mg/L (odds ratio [OR]: 1.62, 95% CI: 1.42-1.85) and were highest among those receiving PIP/TAZ with trough levels ≥17 mg/L (OR: 2.03, 95% CI: 1.36-2.98). Among patients not receiving PIP/TAZ, trough levels ≥17 mg/L were associated with higher AKI odds (OR: 1.43, 95% CI: 1.26-1.63). Concomitant PIP/TAZ identified a population with increased AKI risk across trough strata, whereas the incremental association of a higher trough level was less apparent among PIP/TAZ users. These observational findings support individualized assessment of vancomycin exposure together with concurrent AKI risk factors and should not be interpreted as establishing a new therapeutic trough target.

articles.title: Reversible mitochondrial iron toxicity in Wolfram syndrome type 2 monogenic diabetes.
articles.abstract: CONTEXT: Wolfram syndrome type 2 (WS2) is a rare monogenic diabetes syndrome caused by CISD2 mutations. Its cellular pathophysiology remains poorly understood, and no targeted therapies exist. OBJECTIVE: To characterize the clinical phenotype and cellular pathophysiology of the largest WS2 cohort to date, and to evaluate a novel, mechanistically targeted pharmacological intervention. DESIGN: Observational cohort study paired with ex vivo functional cellular assays and a proof-of-concept pilot clinical intervention. SETTING: Multicenter academic and clinical institutions in Israel and the Palestinian territories. PATIENTS: Twenty-two patients from 11 unrelated Palestinian families presenting with atypical juvenile-onset diabetes and gastrointestinal bleeding. Patient-derived fibroblasts (n = 4) were utilized for functional assays. INTERVENTION(S): Fibroblasts and 2 patients were treated with a combination of the iron chelator deferiprone (DFP) and the antioxidant N-acetylcysteine (NAC). MAIN OUTCOME MEASURE(S): Clinical phenotype, CISD2 genetic analysis, mitochondrial labile iron (mLI) and reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, organelle morphology, and preliminary clinical response (HbA1c, platelet aggregation). RESULTS: Patients were homozygous for a CISD2 c.109G>C founder mutation (carrier rate 1:40). The clinical phenotype was expanded to include prevalent psychiatric morbidity and congenital heart defects. Patient fibroblasts exhibited profound mitochondrial and endoplasmic reticulum damage, with increased mLI (+25%, P < .0001) and mROS (+28%, P < .0001). In vitro DFP-NAC treatment fully reversed these cellular anomalies. In a preliminary pilot study, 2 patients receiving DFP-NAC demonstrated improved reported glycemic control and corrected platelet aggregation. CONCLUSION: WS2 is an underdiagnosed monogenic diabetes driven by mitochondrial iron dysregulation and oxidative stress. Repurposing DFP-NAC reverses this toxicity, offering a strong mechanistic rationale for future clinical trials.
articles.journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism

articles.title: Risk of major adverse cardiovascular events and all-cause mortality across chronic kidney disease stages: A population-based retrospective cohort study in South Korea.
articles.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is associated with increased cardiovascular and all-cause mortality risk. However, few studies have assessed whether these risks vary across CKD stages in Asian populations. Using Korean National Health Insurance data (2016-2020), we analyzed a cohort of 51,352 individuals newly diagnosed with CKD. We compared incidence rates of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and all-cause mortality across CKD stages. Model 1 adjusted for age and sex; Model 2, the primary adjusted model, additionally adjusted for income and health insurance coverage type. All covariates were ascertained on or before cohort entry. During follow-up, 9708 participants (18.9%) experienced MACE and 7091 (13.8%) died. Compared with stage 1 CKD, stage 5 CKD with dialysis was associated with higher hazards of MACE (Model 2 hazard ratio = 4.67; 95% confidence interval = 4.24-5.13) and all-cause mortality (hazard ratio = 5.61; 95% confidence interval = 4.94-6.38). The corresponding incidence rates were 26,148 MACE cases and 16,441 deaths per 100,000 person-years. Advanced CKD stages were associated with higher hazards of MACE and all-cause mortality after adjustment for baseline demographic and socioeconomic characteristics. Residual confounding by clinical characteristics remains possible.

articles.title: Comparison of acute kidney injury after robot-assisted versus laparoscopic partial nephrectomy in high-risk patients: a retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Whether robot-assisted partial nephrectomy (RAPN) reduces acute kidney injury (AKI) compared with laparoscopic partial nephrectomy (LPN) in patients with limited renal reserve remains uncertain. We compared early AKI and six-month renal outcomes between approaches in high-risk patients. METHODS: This single-center retrospective cohort study included adult patients with solitary kidney, documented CKD, or preoperative estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) <60 mL/min/1.73 m2 who underwent laparoscopic or robotic-assisted partial nephrectomy between October 2015 and December 2023. Stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) adjusted for measured baseline differences. The primary outcome was creatinine-defined AKI within 24 h after surgery. Secondary outcomes included AKI stage, intensive care unit (ICU) admission, length of stay, non-AKI complications, and 6-month renal function postoperatively. Sensitivity analyses restricted the cohort to 2021-2023 or applied overlap weighting. RESULTS: Among 227 patients, 76 underwent robotic-assisted partial nephrectomy and 151 underwent laparoscopic partial nephrectomy. After IPTW, 24-hour AKI occurred in 32.4% versus 26.9% (odds ratio [OR] 1.30, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.68-2.49; p = 0.425). AKI stage (common OR 1.27, 95% CI 0.70-2.31; p = 0.435) and ICU admission (20.0% vs 18.1%; p = 0.740) were similar. Operative duration was longer with RAPN (median difference 20.9 min; p < 0.001), whereas clamp time and blood loss were comparable. Postoperative length of stay was 4 versus 5 days (p = 0.058). Six-month eGFR was lower after RAPN (45.9 vs 51.0 mL/min/1.73 m2; median difference -5.1, 95% CI -9.5 to -0.7; p = 0.022), but percentage eGFR decline did not differ (p = 0.299). A > 20% decline occurred in 19.3% versus 9.3% (OR 2.33, 95% CI 1.00-5.45; p = 0.050). The primary AKI finding was consistent in sensitivity analyses. CONCLUSION: In high-risk patients, robotic-assisted partial nephrectomy was not associated with a lower incidence or severity of 24-hour postoperative creatinine-defined AKI compared with LPN. Six-month renal findings were exploratory and warrant confirmation.

articles.title: Regional disparities in clinicopathological characteristics and overall survival after radical nephroureterectomy for upper tract urothelial carcinoma: a multi-institutional cohort study across European and Taiwanese centers.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Upper tract urothelial carcinoma (UTUC) shows marked geographic variation, partly driven by differences in carcinogenic exposures such as smoking and region-specific environmental toxins. These factors may influence tumour characteristics and outcomes. We assessed whether clinicopathologic features and survival differ between patients treated with radical nephroureterectomy (RNU) at European and Taiwanese centres.  METHODS: Data from patients who underwent RNU at 29 centres across Europe and Taiwan were collected. Variable selection for multivariable analysis was performed via LASSO, followed by an adjusted Cox proportional hazards model to identify independent predictors of overall survival (OS). One-to-one propensity score matching (PSM) was applied to balance confounders prior to Kaplan-Meier and restricted mean survival time analyses. KEY FINDINGS AND LIMITATIONS: A total of 2634 patients were included (European: n=2036; Taiwanese: n=598). Taiwanese patients were more often female, had better ECOG performance status, were more frequently never-smokers, had lower clinical T stage, smaller tumours, and more frequently low-grade disease. Treatment patterns also differed, with higher rates of lymphadenectomy and adjuvant chemotherapy in Taiwan, less frequent lymphadenectomy in Europe, and higher positive surgical margin rates in Taiwan. In multivariable analysis, region was not independently associated with OS (HR 1.16, 95% CI 0.95-1.41; p=0.15). Independent predictors of worse OS included older age, worse ECOG, advanced pT stage, nodal involvement, and lymphovascular invasion. OS remained comparable between groups after PSM.  CONCLUSION AND CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS: Despite substantial differences in baseline patient characteristics and treatment patterns, geographic region was not independently associated with OS. Outcomes after RNU appear to be primarily determined by established patient- and tumour-level prognostic factors rather than by geographic origin per se. In this study, we compared patients with upper tract urothelial carcinoma treated in Europe and Taiwan. Although patients in Taiwan had smaller tumours and were generally in better overall health, survival outcomes were similar among comparable patients. These findings suggest that prognosis is driven more by individual patient and tumour characteristics than by geographic differences.

articles.title: Rituximab combined with low-dose, short-course glucocorticoids versus standard glucocorticoid therapy in adults with newly diagnosed minimal change disease: A retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of rituximab (RTX) combined with low-dose, short-course glucocorticoids (GC) in adults with newly diagnosed minimal change disease (MCD). METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 45 adults with newly diagnosed MCD. The RTX group (n=20) received RTX (1 g on days 1 and 15) plus low-dose methylprednisolone (0.25-0.30 mg/kg/day for 3 months). The GC group (n=25) received standard full-dose GCs. Remission rates, relapse rates within 12 months, laboratory parameters, and adverse events were compared. RESULTS: Baseline characteristics were similar. Complete remission (CR) rates were comparable (95% vs. 92%, P>0.05). The relapse rate within 12 months was significantly lower in the RTX group (15% vs. 56%, P=0.004). Serum albumin levels and lipid profiles improved in both groups; renal function remained stable. Cushingoid features were significantly less frequent in the RTX group (5% vs. 84%, P<0.001). No severe adverse events occurred. DISCUSSION: RTX combined with low-dose GCs achieved remission rates comparable to those of standard therapy, with fewer relapses and reduced GC-related toxicity. CONCLUSION: This RTX-based regimen may be a promising first-line alternative for selected patients with newly diagnosed MCD.
